name: 3_CE11684
comments: Authors present 3 VS models obtained from 4 arrays: S1 = MASW only using Array 11684-1, but not used for computing VS30 in their study due to clear lateral velocity variation in the subsurface; S2 = SASW study using Array 11684-2; S3 = model from combined SASW (Array 11684-3) and MASW (11684-4) data.

name: 11_CE13922
comments: The user is recommended to read comments in Appendix A of the original study. From the authors: "The VS model (Model 1 [S1]) provided to represent subsurface velocity structure has bedrock interpreted at an intermediate depth of 13 m with alternate interpretations having bedrock in the 11 to 16 m depth range being viable. Inversion of the Love wave dispersion data (or for that matter Rayleigh wave data) is unable to accurately model the VS of the half space (i.e. bedrock) and, in this case, appears to significantly underestimate bedrock velocity relative to P- and S-wave refraction data. Therefore, an alternate model (Model 2 [S2]) is presented with bedrock VS fixed at 1,600 m/s, which is still expected to be conservative. This model has higher RMS error, but still falls within the scatter in the dispersion data, expect at longest wavelengths, which may have underestimated phase velocity due to near field effects."

name: 16_CE23063
comments: The authors generated three VS models from the surface wave data: Model 1 (S1) using only MASW dispersion data, Model 2 (S2) using MASW dispersion data and <U+201C>L<U+201D> array passive surface wave data at wavelengths of less than 120 m (before gap in passive surface wave dispersion data), and Model 3 (S3) using MASW and all <U+201C>L<U+201D> array passive surface wave data.

name: 20_CE24644
comments: The authors present two VS models from MASW dispersion data: a model with a minimal number of layers resulting in a large impedance contrast at 17 m depth (S1), and a model with gradual increase in velocity with depth after a large velocity increase at 13 m (S2).

name: 21_CE24706
comments: The authors present 4 VS models: two using data combined from passive array 24706-1 and MASW array 24706-3, with assumed Poisson's ratios of 0.25 and 0.3 (Models S1A and S1B), respectively; and two models using the L-Shaped Passive Array 24706-1/2, with assumed Poisson's ratios of 0.25 and 0.3 (Models S2A and S2B), respectively. All models assume average mode of surface wave propagation. The authors have "assumed that Model 2 (A and B) generated from the passive L-shaped array, which is closer to the free field seismic station, is most representative of seismic station conditions. A Poisson<U+2019>s ratio of 0.3 is more realistic than 0.25, especially if fractured rock is saturated and, therefore, Model 2B, with VS30 of 468 m/s, is considered most representative of site conditions."

name: 117_CITEH

name: 120_CITIN
comments:
Because of the variable depth beneath the array, five models were developed for the
MASW data set to explore the variation in VS30. Model 1 (S1) fits the representative
dispersion curve and is, therefore, considered the average VS model for the array. Model 2 (S2) fits the lower envelope of the dispersion data and based on the passive surface wave
data collected along array TIN-1 is expected to be most representative of seismic station
conditions. Model 3 (S3) fits the upper and lower envelope of the dispersion data at small and long wavelengths, respectively. Model 4 (S4) fits the upper envelope of the dispersion data. Model 5 (S5) fits the lower and upper envelope of the dispersion data at small and long wavelengths.

name: 121_CITOR

name: 130_CIWNS
comments:
The authors indicate that two separate attempts to characterize this site with non-invasive methods were unsuccessful. They instead refer to a VS profile obtained from PS Suspension logging as performed for the <U+201C>Resolution of Site Response Issues from the Northridge Earthquake (ROSRINE)<U+201D> Project. The authors indicate that the PS suspension log data "did not accurately characterize
velocity structure in the upper 2 m. MASW data were reviewed and near surface
sediment/fill S-wave velocity was found to be about 225 m/s. ... VS30 was estimated from the PS suspension log R1-R2 analysis using a VS of 225 m/s for the upper 2.25 m, based on MASW data, and is 1,043 m/s (NEHRP Site Class B). [The authors] recommend using this estimate of VS30 for site characterization."
